name: Gān Dèng Yǎn 干瞪眼
description: Gan Deng Yan is a Chinese climbing and shedding game in which most responses must be exactly one rank higher than the previous combination. Players begin with small hands, draw from a talon after each trick, and try to be first to shed all cards.

overview.description: Gan Deng Yan is a Chinese climbing and shedding game in which most responses must be exactly one rank higher than the previous combination. Players begin with small hands, draw from a talon after each trick, and try to be first to shed all cards.

history.origins: Gan Deng Yan emerged in southwest China during the early to mid-2010s, with reported roots in Sichuan and documented play in Yunnan variants.
timeline: 2010s: Emerged in Sichuan (Shudi), China; spread to Yunnan and across China.

setup.players: 2 to 6 players, with each player competing individually.
setup.dealing: Dealer shuffles, then players draw cards in counterclockwise order until dealer has 6 cards and each other player has 5. Remaining cards form a face-down talon.

rules.objective: Be the first player to shed all cards from hand; if you cannot win, minimize cards left when another player goes out.
rules.gameplay: Play proceeds in tricks. A lead may be a legal ordinary combination or bomb. Each following play must be the same combination type and exactly one rank higher, or a permitted special response such as a two-set on singles/pairs, or a bomb. Players may pass. When all but one player pass, the trick ends; players draw from the talon starting with the last player to play, then that player leads the next trick.
keyRules: Singles, pairs, sequences, and double-sequences are ordinary combinations; responses must usually be exactly one rank higher.
Twos are highest in singles and pairs but cannot be used inside sequences or double-sequences.
Bombs (triples, four-of-a-kind, and double-joker bomb) can beat ordinary combinations, with larger bomb classes beating smaller ones.
Jokers are wild in combinations but cannot normally be played as single cards unless it is your only remaining card when leading.

strategy.basic: Preserve flexible middle ranks so you can answer exact one-step climbs instead of passing too early.
strategy.intermediate: Track talon depth and trick timing: winning a trick near the end of talon can secure lead control without feeding opponents extra draws.
strategy.advanced: Use bombs as tempo tools rather than panic plays; forcing passes at the right moment can create a clean lead where you unload multiple combinations in sequence.
tips: Avoid spending twos too early unless they secure critical lead control.
Plan around exact-step responses: a gap in rank often means forced pass even with strong cards.
Count likely bomb density from exposed plays before committing a high ordinary combination.

variations.name: Double-Deck Group Play
variations.description: Some groups use two 54-card packs for larger player counts, increasing hand volume and reducing early talon exhaustion.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variant only changes deck count and joker colour rules; no engine constant overrides documented in source.

variations.name: Triplets as Ordinary Combinations
variations.description: Some tables treat triplets as ordinary combinations rather than bombs, allowing one-step triplet responses.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Would require custom combination and bomb rules; exact engine overrides not specified in source.

scoring.description: Winner scores one point from each opponent for every card that opponent still holds at the end of the deal.

synthesis.shortDescription: Chinese climbing/shedding game where players play combinations that beat the previous play or pass.
